(Times of Ceylon.)
Paris, Sept. 14.
The “Auto” learns that the Rugby Unions of Australia and New Zealand have officially asked the French Rugby Federation whether it would welcome representative teams in 1926-27.

It is impossible for the Federation to receive both teams simultaneously, but it is understood that it has agreed to invite the Australians in 1926-27 and the New Zealanders during 1927-28 to play a number of matches in Paris and the provinces.

RUGBY RULES.
INTERNATIONAL BOARD'S CHANGES.
SCRUMS, OFFSIDE, THROW-OUT.

In order that all players may familiarise themselves with the changes in the laws of the game recently passed by the International Board, the Home Rugby Union have just issued a resume of such changes.

In regard to a scrummage, the team not responsible for the stoppage now has the right of putting the ball into the scrummage on either side, and the ball is not to be considered fairly in the scrummage until it has passed a player on each side.
An offside player is not to be put onside when the ball is touched by an opponent, but only when the ball is intentionally so touched. No charge is to be allowed when a penalty kick is taken.
Another interesting change is in the throw-out law. The ball must now be thrown out so as to alight at least five yards at right angles to the touch-line.

"CELL SHOCK."
MURDERER'S LIFE SAVED BY IT
The term “cell shock” was written into the practice of American jurisprudence. by a Chicago jury.
Through it, Russell Scott, a Canadian millionaire at thirty and later a bootlegger and bandit, escaped the gallows for the murder of a chemist's clerk in a Chicago hold-up.

Scott, who lost his fortune in attempting to promote an international bridge between Windsor and Detroit, has thrice escaped the gallows. In the first two instances eleventh-hour reprieves from the Executive saved his life when an appeal to the highest courts had failed. These two narrow escapes, Scott's friends declared, unbalanced his mind.
Through the tireless efforts of a loyal wife and father, a writ of habeas corpus was obtained, granting him a jury test as to his sanity.

Although prison officials and attendants and five alienists declared Scott to be sane, the jury gave a verdict supporting the contention of five other alienists that such narrow escapes from death were enough to unbalance the strongest man, and Scott was not strong mentally and had become insane.
Following the jury's verdict, from which no appeal is possible, Scott has been committed to the State insane asylum, but with the proviso that if he ever becomes sane he must be executed.

The hearing was resumed at Marlborough Street of the summons against Charles Robinson, of the Coventry Club, Denman Street, Piccadilly, for assaulting Mr. Charles Hutton Moss, inquiry agent, of St. James's Street, Piccadilly.

Robinson was the plaintiff in the recent claim against the Midland Bank which was known as the "Mr. A." case. Mr. Moss was employed by the bank in connection with that action and at the previous hearing he alleged that when he went to the Coventry Club with a Mr. Starkie, Robinson struck him a number of blows.
Mr. Vine, defending: Did you ask Robinson for a large sum of money, in connection with the Midland Bank case?
Mr. Moss: He offered me 25 per cent. if I would assist him, but I had already given full information to Scotland Yard and the bank.
Did you not say you would give him information if he would allow you £5,000 in the event of the action going in his favour?—Never.
Richard William Starkie, of Oakley-square, N.W., said he took Mr. Moss to the Coventry Club. Mr. Moss walked towards the bar and then saw him and Robinson having a fight.
Cross-examined by Mr. Vine, Mr. Starkie said when he tried to pacify him Moss said:—

You don't know me. I am the most reverigeful- and vindictive person that you have ever met. This assault is going to be of very great use to me. I have an action pending against the Midland Bank for $5,000. It is going to be important because it is going to prove that I am going about in fear of my life. I will see that that man gets six months.
An “Outrageous” Action.
Mr. Keeves, prosecuting: Did you say that you did not wish to give evidence?—Yes.

Did you say you were trying to get back on the medical register?
—No.

Robinson, giving evidence, said he met Moss on several occasions in connection with his action. Immediately he saw Moss he told Mr. Starkie he had no right to bring Moss into the club and to take him out at once.

Moss at once held up a stick and tried to strike him. He warded off the stick, which hit his shoulder, and struck Moss. It was not true that two men held Moss while he rained blows on him. He considered that Moss, who was the aggressor, was an undesirable person to be in the club.

Mr. Mead: Why did you take it upon yourself to say who should be turned out of the club? Was it not an outrageous thing to address a fellow-member in that way?—No, I do not think so. In the absence of an official of the club I think it was right for me to protest.
Mr. Samuel E. Williams, a solicitor and member of the Coventry Club, said he saw Moss raise his stick to hit Robinson. Then Robinson let out with his fists.
Mr. George Harris, secretary of the Coventry Club, said both men were striking at each other. Robinson probably struck two or three blows.
Replying to Mr. Mead, Mr. Harris agreed it was outrageous conduct for Robinson to have interfered with a member who brought in a guest he did not like.
Mr. Mead: Is that tolerated in this high-class club?—No. The matter is coming before the committee after this case has been decided.
TRADE ROMANCE

The enterprise of these responsible for the founding of the English India Company and the patented and bravery of those responsible for carrying on its work forms the subject of an article in the Scottish Educational Journal. The story whilst being of educational value, it states, is also sufficiently colourful to attract the youthful student. After dealing with the first efforts of London merchants to secure a portion of the profitable business which was being carried on in the East India by the Portuguese and Dutch and the bestowal on them by Queen Elizabeth of a special monopoly, the efforts of the leading members of the association to obtain funds for the equipping of a commercial squadron are referred to. Large numbers shrank from the risk, and at last there was nothing for it but to create a separate association of the more enterprising and start business on much smaller scale than was originally intended.

On February 18, 1601, therefore, five small ships, the largest of which was only 600 tons, weighed anchor at Tor Bay, and steered on that amazing course which was to lead to the conquest of an empire. Of the many adventuring banks that have left our shores, not one has opened a story to equal the strangeness, the romance, the magnificence, of the events that were ushered in by the sailing of those five ships. Patience must have been one of the finest assets of the little group of merchants who undertook the first expedition, for they had to wait two years and seven months before their ships came home. Captain James Lancaster, under whose command they had sailed, had already been in India, but so slightly was he acquainted with the geography of the regions into which his argosies were sailing that he did not reach his destination. Acheen in Sumatra, till June 5, 1602—one year and a half after leaving England. In spite of successful business done, the wake of his five ships was not followed with much enthusiasm, the result being that for about ten years no great advance was made. Then, in 1812, a Captain Best secured privileges from the ruler at Delhi, which included the right to establish a factory at Surat, and the connection with the mainland thus made, was greatly strengthened three years later, when James I. sent Sir Thomas Roe as his ambassador to Delhi. He was received with the highest honours, and English trade with India was much encouraged. But in viewing the story of the advance of the British in the land of the Moguls, we have always to bear in mind that the distance between the two scenes of the Company's activities, together with ever changing circumstance in both places, did much to dislocate their arrangements. While the pioneers, far from the home base, were opening up fresh sources of prosperity, the Governor and his Directors in London were facing and overcoming a variety of difficulties. Increasing success (somewhat slow, however), brought competitors into the field who sought to ignore the Charter which James I. had renewed; and these competitors were not discouraged by Charles I. In spite of the monopoly that the Company legally possessed, the King last named—doubtless on account of his own need for money—granted a second Charter to a separate association, and the trade thus divided was of little profit to either, till they were finally amalgamated into one company.

SCOUTS RESCUE.
MADE FAST AND HANDED OVER
Off St. Bses Head, Cumberland, one Saturday five Boy Scouts saved a coasting steamer from running around on the rocky east.

In the early hours off the morning the steamship "Linton," of Cardiff (324 tons), left Working ton for Bambrugh Pool with cargo of gravel. Fog and rain were encountered, and between Whitehaven and St. Bees Head crew of eight left the vessel in the ship's small boat.
They landed at Barrowmouth near Whitehaven, and, guided by the light of St. Bees lighthouse, climbed the sliffs and reached the lighthouse in an exhausted condition at seven o'clock.

The 10th Halifax Scouts and Hensingham (Cumberland) Rovers Scouts, who were encamped at St Bees, saw the "Linton" drifting helplessly about a mile from shore. Three hours later the Scoutes decided to conduct salvage operations. Scoutmaster the Rev. Roseveare, of Halifax, selected four strong swimmers to accompany him in a rowing boat. These were Assistant Scoutmaster Denton, Patrol Leader Fletcher of Halifax, and Rovers Watson and Wilson, of Hensingham, alleged between 16 and 20.

Great difficulty was experienced in launching the boat owing to the heavy surf. Several times it nearly capsized and the occupants who were clad in shorts and vests were drenched. Eventually good progress was made, and an hour later the Scouts boarded the steamer. This was no sooner accomplished than the rowing boat was dashed against the ship's side and sank.

The Scouts made the steamer fast by dropping the anchors.
In the meantime the harbour authorities at Whitehaven had been informed of the situation. The Linton's crew were transported to Whitehaven and taken in a Whitehaven tug to the anchored steamer. Here a transfer was effected, the crew replacing the Scouts. The Linton, under her own steam, went to Whitehaven.
On arrival back in camp the Scouts were given a rousing reception by their comrades.
Mr. Roseveare told a reporter he intended to claim salvage and, if successful, to devote the money to the erection of new Sunday schools in the parish of St. Paul's, King's Cross, Halifax, and to furthering the Scout movement.
